contribution.value: Introduces LAMBADA, a word prediction benchmark of 10,022 narrative passages where the last word is guessable only with broad discourse context, not the final sentence alone.

ev.quote: We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task.
The LAMBADA dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages
The LAMBADA data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015).

datasets.value: Control set (5K passages from BookCorpus test novels)

ev.quote: This control set was constructed by randomly sampling 5K passages of the same shape and size as the ones used to build LAMBADA from the same test novels

data_size.value: 10,022 passages (4,869 dev + 5,153 test); training corpus of 2,662 novels with 203 million words; total novel pool 5,325 books and 465 million words

ev.quote: The LAMBADA dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages (extracted from 1,331 and 1,332 disjoint novels, respectively).
a Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM) (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997)
a traditional statistical N-Gram language model (Stolcke, 2002) with and without cache
a traditional statistical N-Gram language model (Stolcke, 2002) with and without cache
and a Memory Network (Sukhbaatar et al., 2015)
we constructed Sup-CBOW, a baseline model weakly tailored to the task at hand, consisting of a simple neural network
We also considered an unsupervised variant (Unsup-CBOW) where the target word is predicted by cosine similarity
the measure of interest for LAMBADA is the average success of a model at predicting the target word, i.e., accuracy
as we observe a bottoming effect with accuracy, we also report perplexity and median rank of correct word
we also report perplexity and median rank of correct word, to better compare the models

key_results.value: On LAMBADA, no tested language model reaches above 1% accuracy (LSTM, RNN, Memory Network, N-Gram all 0%; N-Gram w/cache 0.1%)

ev.quote: none of several state-ofthe-art language models reaches accuracy above 1% on this novel benchmark

key_results.value: N-Gram with cache achieves the best LAMBADA perplexity at 768 (still 0.1% accuracy)

ev.quote: the best relative performance on LAMBADA is achieved by N-Gram w/cache, which takes passage statistics into account. While even this model is effectively unable to guess the right word, it achieves a respectable perplexity of 768.

key_results.value: Random capitalized word from passage baseline reaches 7.3% accuracy on LAMBADA, beating all neural models

ev.quote: We thus propose LAMBADA as a challenging test set, meant to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context
We introduce LAMBADA, a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding
We gratefully acknowledge the support of NVIDIA Corporation with the donation of the GPUs used in our research.

strengths.value: Human-validated by strict crowdsourcing: each passage requires two consecutive subjects to guess the target with broad context, but no subject from a pool of ten can guess from the last sentence.

ev.quote: We required two consecutive subjects to exactly match the missing word, and we made sure that no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only

strengths.value: Casts long-context understanding as standard word prediction, so any language model can be tested without task-specific architecture changes.

ev.quote: LAMBADA casts language understanding in the classic word prediction framework of language modeling.

strengths.value: Built from unpublished BookCorpus novels, which limits leakage of world knowledge from Wikipedia or famous books.

ev.quote: The fact that it contains unpublished novels minimizes the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources for the task

strengths.value: Establishes a wide gap between humans and 2016 language models (all under 1% accuracy), giving a clear long-term research target.

ev.quote: none of several state-ofthe-art language models reaches accuracy above 1% on this novel benchmark

weaknesses.value: Authors call the modelling work very preliminary and a proof-of-concept, with limited tuning of neural baselines.

ev.quote: the evaluation we performed is very preliminary, and it must only be taken as a proof-of-concept study of the difficulty of LAMBADA.

weaknesses.value: Filtering selects passages where simple language models already fail, so standard LMs are bound to score near zero by design.

ev.quote: standard language models are bound to fail on it by design: one of our first filters (see Section 3.1) was to choose passages where a number of simple language models were failing

weaknesses.value: Strict perfect-match acceptance rule rejects synonyms or other plausible continuations, narrowing what counts as a correct answer.

ev.quote: An alternative to this perfect-match approach would have been to include passages where broad-context subjects provided other plausible or synonymous continuations.

weaknesses.value: Cost limited the use of more annotators at stage 1, which the authors say could improve filtering quality.

ev.quote: Cost considerations also precluded us from using more subjects at stage 1, which could in principle improve the quality of filtering at this step.

limitations.value: Single language only: LAMBADA covers English narrative fiction, with no multilingual or multi-domain coverage.

ev.quote: in contrast to other kinds of texts like news data, Wikipedia text, or famous novels

limitations.value: Skews heavily toward proper nouns (48% of targets), so the benchmark partly tests co-reference rather than full discourse reasoning.

ev.quote: Figure 2(b) shows that most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and, at a distance, verbs (7.7%).

limitations.value: Reports no statistical confidence intervals, no inter-annotator agreement scores, and no multiple training seeds for the model results.

ev.quote: Results of models and baselines are reported in Table 1.

limitations.value: Does not evaluate any modern (post-2016) Transformer or large pretrained model, only classic RNN, LSTM, n-gram, and Memory Network baselines.

ev.quote: We implemented a simple RNN (Elman, 1990), a Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM) (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997), a traditional statistical N-Gram language model

future_work_stated.value: Launch a public competition based on the LAMBADA data to push community progress.

ev.quote: we plan to announce a public competition based on the LAMBADA data.

future_work_stated.value: Develop new long-term memory and reasoning models that can retrieve broad-context information.

ev.quote: the ability to store information in a longer-term memory will be a crucial component of successful models, coupled with the ability to perform some kind of reasoning

future_work_stated.value: Add attention mechanisms or more extensive hyperparameter tuning to the baseline models.

ev.quote: Better results might be obtained simply by performing more extensive tuning, by adding more sophisticated mechanisms such as attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014)

future_work_stated.value: Further analysis of why dialogic / direct-speech passages are over-represented in LAMBADA items.

ev.quote: Further analysis is needed to investigate in what way more dialogic discourse might facilitate the prediction of the final target word.
The average passage consists of 4.6 sentences in the context plus 1 target sentence, for a total length of 75.4 tokens (dev) / 75 tokens (test).
The development set of LAMBADA, along with the training corpus, can be downloaded at http://clic. cimec.unitn.it/lambada/.
